# Volume 2 — VII The Pointing of Duty

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Nell reclined in her chair and let out a sigh on a temperate evening in October. She occupied a seat beside a table that was laden with exercise books and textbooks, yet the pages in front of her, filled with dense writing, seemed to have no relation to school work or studies.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0000 }

“What is the matter?” asked Hugh, who had reached the unclosed door of the kitchen right when the sigh was uttered.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0001 }

Nell blushed, shoving her written work from view beneath a few school papers.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0002 }

“It is not anything too terrible. Following Professor Hamilton's counsel, I attempted to draft a few of my ideas, yet I was unable to make them satisfy me. The moment they are recorded using black ink on white paper, they appear terribly motionless and silly. Whims resemble shadows . . . they are such untamed, leaping entities that you are unable to imprison them. Still, if I persist in my efforts, maybe I will master the trick eventually. As you are aware, my free time is quite limited. When I complete the grading of school assignments and essays, I am not always in the mood to compose something of my own.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0003 }

“Nell, your progress at school is going wonderfully. You are liked by all the children,” Hugh said, as he seated himself upon the stone step.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0004 }

“No, not entirely. Anthony Tulk does not and will not like me. Worse still, he lacks respect for me . . . no, he really does not. He merely regards me with disdain, and I am not ashamed to admit to you that this distresses me terribly. It is not because he is particularly wicked . . . he is merely somewhat cheeky, though no more so than a few of the rest. He rarely defies my commands; yet he complies with a disdainful look of endurance, as though contesting the matter were not worth his time or else he would . . . and this influences the rest negatively. I have attempted all possible means to gain his favor, but I am starting to worry that I never will. I wish to, because he is a fairly clever young boy, even if he is a Tulk, and I might affectionally regard him if he allowed me to.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0005 }

“It is likely just the result of what is said in his household.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0006 }

“Not entirely. Anthony is a self-reliant young fellow who forms his own opinions regarding matters. He has continually been taught by male instructors in the past and he claims female educators are useless. Anyway, we will observe what can be achieved through patience and gentle care. Tackling obstacles appeals to me, and instructing children is truly quite fascinating labor. Cedric Stanhope compensates for everything that is absent in the rest. That youngster is an absolute treasure, Hugh, as well as a brilliant mind. I am convinced that society will learn about his talents in the future,” Nell finished with a voice full of certainty.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0007 }

“Teaching is something I enjoy as well,” Hugh remarked. “For a start, it serves as excellent preparation. Really, Nell, during these weeks spent instructing the youth of Pale Sands, I have acquired more knowledge than throughout my entire time as a student. Everything appears to be progressing smoothly for us. Word has reached me that Odette is well-liked by those in Stonebridge; meanwhile, I believe Pale Sands finds your obedient servant reasonably acceptable . . . save for Mr. Andrew Tranter. While returning home yesterday evening, I encountered Mrs. Peter Scobie, who mentioned feeling obligated to let me know that Mr. Tranter was dissatisfied with my approach.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0008 }

“Have you ever observed,” Nell asked in a thoughtful tone, “that whenever individuals declare it to be their duty to inform you of something, you can expect an unpleasant revelation? For what reason do they never appear to consider it a duty to relay the nice remarks they hear regarding you? Mrs. H. B. Trask paid another visit to the school yesterday and said she felt it her duty to notify me that Mrs. Gorham Pullen disapproved of my reading fairy tales to the pupils, and that Mr. Rogerson believed Prillie was not progressing quickly enough in arithmetic. Were Prillie to devote less time to flirting with the boys over her slate, she could make better progress. I am fairly certain that Jack Pettigrew solves her class arithmetic problems for her, even if I have failed to catch him in the act.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0009 }

“Did you manage to make the optimistic son of Mrs. Trask accept his holy name?”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0010 }

“Yes,” Nell chuckled, “yet the undertaking was truly hard. In the beginning, he refused to pay the slightest attention when I addressed him as ‘St. Clair’ until I had repeated it two or three times; after which, as the other boys poked him, he would glance upward wearing a terribly offended expression, as though I had referred to him as John or Wilfred and he could not possibly realize I was addressing him. Therefore, I detained him after classes one evening to speak with him gently. I explained that his mother desired me to address him as St. Clair and I was unable to act contrary to her desires. Once everything was fully laid out he understood . . . he is actually quite a sensible little boy . . . and he stated that I had permission to address him as St. Clair, though he would ‘lick the stuffing’ from any boy who attempted to do so. Naturally, I was obliged to scold him once more for employing such awful phrasing. From that time on I address him as St. Clair while the boys address him as Jake, and everything proceeds without trouble. He tells me he intends to become a carpenter, whereas Mrs. Trask instructs me to turn him into a college professor.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0011 }

Hugh’s train of thought shifted to another path when college was brought up, and for a while the two of them conversed about their hopes and intentions . . . seriously, solemnly, with optimism, in the manner that young people enjoy conversing, when what lies ahead remains an unexplored trail brimming with amazing potential.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0012 }

Hugh had at last decided that he would become a doctor.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0013 }

“It is a wonderful career,” he declared with passion. “Throughout existence, a person must battle against something . . . was it not once stated that man is a combative creature? . . . and my desire is to battle illness and suffering and lack of knowledge . . . which are entirely interconnected. Nell, I desire to contribute my portion of genuine, sincere labor to this earth . . . contribute a tiny bit to the total of human understanding that every noble person has collected since the start of time. Those who existed prior to my time have accomplished a great deal for my benefit, so I desire to demonstrate my appreciation by accomplishing something for those who will exist following my time. In my view, that represents the sole method a person can settle his debts to humanity.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0014 }

“My wish is to bring more beauty into the world,” Nell remarked with a dreamy tone. “Increasing people's knowledge isn't quite my goal . . . even if I recognize that as the highest aim . . . rather, I would delight in giving them a more enjoyable experience through my presence . . . in sparking some modest happiness or cheerful feeling that wouldn't have come to pass had I not come into existence.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0015 }

“I believe you achieve that goal daily,” Hugh remarked with admiration.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0016 }

And he spoke the truth. Nell belonged among the children of light by right of birth. Once she had traversed a life, casting a smile or a word over it like a beam of sunlight, the possessor of that life perceived it, at least temporarily, as full of hope, beautiful, and commendable.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0017 }

At last Hugh stood up with reluctance.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0018 }

“Well, I need to hurry over to MacPhersons’,” I said. “Elias Purdy returned from Regent’s today to spend Sunday, and he was supposed to carry out a book that Professor Garrick is loaning to me.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0019 }

“Furthermore, I need to prepare Thirza’s tea. Since she departed to visit Mrs. Farrow earlier tonight, her return will happen shortly.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0020 }

Upon Thirza's return, tea had been prepared by Nell; lively snaps came from the burning fire, a jar containing pale, frosted ferns alongside dark red maple leaves decorated the table, and delicious scents of toast and ham filled the room. Thirza, however, let out a heavy sigh as she dropped into her chair.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0021 }

“Do your eyes bother you? Is your head aching?” Nell asked with concern.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0022 }

“No. I’m just exhausted . . . and concerned. It’s regarding Mary and those children . . . Mary has gotten worse . . . she cannot survive much longer. And regarding the twins, I do not know what will happen to them.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0023 }

“Is there no news from their uncle?”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0024 }

“Yes, Mary received a letter from him. He is employed at a lumber camp and ‘shacking it,’ regardless of what that implies. At any rate, he states that taking the children before the spring is an absolute impossibility for him. He anticipates being married at that time and will possess a home where he can bring them; however, he states that she has to find some neighbors who will harbor them during the winter. She states that asking any of them is something she cannot endure. Mary never was on particularly good terms with the East Welby people, and that is the truth. And the upshot of the whole matter, Nell, is that I am certain Mary desires that I take those children . . . she did not state it outright, but her expression conveyed it.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0025 }

“Oh!” Nell brought her hands together, filled with intense excitement. “And surely you are going to, Thirza, aren’t you?”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0026 }

“My decision is not yet made,” Thirza replied somewhat sharply. “Nell, I do not leap into matters with your impetuous style. Being third cousins provides a rather weak basis. Furthermore, taking charge of a pair of six-year-old youngsters will represent a terrible obligation . . . especially since they are twins.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0027 }

Thirza held the belief that a pair of twins was simply double the trouble of an individual child.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0028 }

“Twins are quite fascinating . . . or a single set of them, anyway,” Nell remarked. “Only upon having a second or third set does it become tedious. Furthermore, I believe it would be truly lovely if you possessed an activity to keep you entertained while I am off at school.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0029 }

“I don’t suppose it would offer much fun . . . I’d expect it to bring more anxiety and trouble than anything. The danger wouldn’t be as great if their ages matched yours when I brought you in. Lucy wouldn’t concern me as deeply . . . she appears well-behaved and calm. But Robin is a handful.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0030 }

Nell possessed a fondness for children, and her heart went out to the Farrow twins. Her memory retained a very vivid picture of her own neglected youth. Knowing that Thirza could only be reached through her uncompromising commitment to what she considered her duty, Nell cleverly aligned her arguments to appeal to this principle.
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0031 }

“Should Robin be misbehaving, that makes it even more necessary for him to receive proper discipline, doesn't it, Thirza? Should we refuse to take them, their destination remains unknown, as do the sorts of conditions that might encompass them. Imagine if they were taken in by Mrs. Farrow’s next door neighbors, the Sprotts. According to Mrs. Sowerby, Henry Sprott utters more profanity than anyone who ever lived, and his children's words are entirely untrustworthy. Would it not be awful if such habits were acquired by the twins? Alternatively, imagine their going to the Wiggins’. As Mrs. Sowerby tells it, Mr. Wiggins converts everything sellable on the property into cash and raises his household using skim milk. You surely would not wish starvation upon your kin, even if your connection is merely that of third cousins, would you? It strikes me, Thirza, as our obligation to accept them.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0032 }

“I guess that’s true,” Thirza agreed dejectedly. “I suppose I will inform Mary that I’m going to accept them. There is no reason for you to appear so thrilled, Nell. This is going to result in a large amount of additional labor for you. My eyes prevent me from doing any sewing whatsoever, which means the responsibility of crafting and repairing their garments will fall to you. And sewing is not something you enjoy.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0033 }

“I detest it,” Nell remarked placidly, “however, if you are prepared to accept those children out of a feeling of duty, I certainly am able to perform their sewing out of a feeling of duty. It benefits people to be required to execute tasks they dislike . . . within reason.”
{: #nw-v02-c07-p0034 }
